podcast.title: Parents' Divorce (1976)
podcast.body: His parents, Jim and Virginia Grohl, divorced in 1976 when Dave was approximately seven years old, a separation that limited the influence of his father's conservative political views on him. "The marriage to Virginia fell apart when Dave was about seven. This was 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Pivotal B-52s Moment (1980)
podcast.body: At age 11, on January 26, 1980, while watching Saturday Night Live with his older sister Lisa, he witnessed The B-52s perform "Rock Lobster." This performance profoundly impacted him, changing his life and inspiring him to embrace "weirdness" in music. "I remember that moment like some people remember the Kennedy assassination. That moment changed my life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: First Guitar (1981)
podcast.body: Received his first guitar for Christmas in 1981, a 1963 Silvertone model from Sears that notably had an amplifier built directly into its case. "Mom got him his first guitar for Christmas in 1981. It was a 1963 Silvertone from Sears with the amp built into the case."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: First Concert Experience (1982/83)
podcast.body: Attended his first live band performance at around age 13 (either 1982 or 1983) at the Cubby Bear in Chicago, where he saw Naked Ray Gun and Rights of the Accused, an experience facilitated by his cousin Tracy. "So the first show I'd ever seen was, it was Naked Ray Gunn and rights of the accused at a place called the Cubby Bear in Chicago."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Transition to Drums (1985)
podcast.body: Around his 16th birthday in January 1985, as Freak Baby evolved into Mission Impossible, Dave Grohl transitioned from guitar to playing the drums. "By this time, David moved to Drums, and this is where we finally get to Dave's earliest recordings that we can find."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Joining Scream (1987)
podcast.body: In 1987, he became a fan of the DC hardcore band Scream. Upon seeing a notice for a new drummer at a music store, he contacted the band, auditioned, and secured what he considered his "dream gig" by the end of the month, replacing their long-time drummer. "He tore the note down, contacted the band, auditioned, and got what he thought was his dream gig by the end of that month."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Harling Talks AD Alias (1990)
podcast.body: In the summer of 1990, while still with Scream, Dave Grohl recorded new demos on his own, creating the alias "Harling Talks Angel Divine," or "Harling Talks AD" for short. With assistance from Barrett Jones and Toss Newyn Huizen, he recorded experimental material that he never expected to go anywhere, and there was never a "Harling Talks show." "Dave created a new alias, he called Harling Talks Angel Divine or Harling Talks AD for short."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Joining Nirvana (1990)
podcast.body: In September 1990, after his band Scream unexpectedly broke up mid-tour, leaving him stranded in Los Angeles, Dave Grohl sought drumming opportunities by calling his friend Buzz Osborne of The Melvins. Osborne facilitated a connection to Nirvana, leading to Grohl's successful audition at the Dutchman rehearsal space in Seattle on September 25, 1990, where he "got the gig instantly." "The day Dave Grohl unexpectedly got the gig with this weird little band called Nirvana, September 25th, 1990."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

podcast.title: Joining Nirvana (1990)
podcast.body: A few months after recording his Harling Talks AD demos, Dave Grohl received a call to audition for Nirvana. Scream had broken up over "girlfriend troubles" while on tour, leaving Dave stranded in Los Angeles. Buzz Osborne of The Melvins, who was idolized by Kurt Cobain, recommended Dave for the open drummer position. Dave flew to Seattle, arriving on Friday, September 21, 1990, and after an informal audition, became a member of the band without any explicit invitation, simply because "they just didn't ask him to leave." "Dave packed his kit into a large cardboard box and boarded a flight for Seattle, arriving on Friday, September 21, 1990."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Post-Scream Legal Issue (1990)
podcast.body: After joining Nirvana and the band signed to DGC, Dave Grohl was sued for $40,000 by someone associated with Scream. This legal action alleged that Dave was still under contract to Scream due to an agreement he signed at some point during his time with them, even though Scream had already broken up. Fortunately, Dave had lawyers who were able to deal with the situation. "Dave was immediately sued by someone associated with Scream for $40,000 saying that he was still under contract to them, even though Scream had long broken up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Pre-Nirvana Demos (1990)
podcast.body: Dave Grohl began recording his own song demos as early as 1990, even before he officially joined Nirvana. These early recordings showcased his ambition beyond being a drummer and eventually led to the release of his cassette-only album "Pocket Watch" under the moniker Late. "Dave recorded some demos as far back as 1990, even before he was with Nirvana."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Deep Depression Post-Nirvana (1994)
podcast.body: Following Kurt Cobain's death in April 1994, Dave Grohl entered a period of deep depression and was unsure of his future in music. He seriously considered quitting music entirely or joining another band, having received invitations from Danzig and Tom Petty. However, he realized he didn't want to be "just a drummer," as playing drums would constantly remind him of his time in Nirvana, a painful memory at that point. "Give it up music actually was an option for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Encouragement from Seven Year Bitch Postcard (1994)
podcast.body: The deciding factor in Dave Grohl's decision to continue making music after Kurt Cobain's suicide was a postcard he received from the Seattle band Seven Year Bitch. The band had endured significant tragedy themselves, losing a member to an overdose in 1992 and another to kidnapping, rape, and murder in 1993, yet they continued to make music. Their postcard read, "We know what you're going through. The desire to play music is gone for now, but it will return. Don't worry." This message convinced Dave that he was "put on this planet to make music" and that stopping would be wrong. "This convinced Dave that he needed to keep going."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Limited Demo Distribution and Bootlegging (1994)
podcast.body: Dave Grohl initially pressed up only 100 vinyl copies of his Pre-Foo Fighters demo sessions, distributing them solely among friends, including Nirvana's tour manager Cristobus Selch and record company confidants. There were also "ultra-ware cassettes" featuring rough mixes of 15 songs. These limited-edition recordings were immediately bootlegged, leading to a surge of record label offers for Dave. "The copies of these sessions were pressed up on vinyl, just a hundred copies, and distributed amongst friends."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Pre-Foo Fighters Demos (1994)
podcast.body: In October 1994, Dave Grohl booked six days of studio time in Seattle with Barrett Jones to record demos, playing all instruments himself. His sole purpose for these sessions was to "prove to himself that he could do it, that he could still make music," without any intention of pursuing a record contract. He would record his drum parts, then move to the control room for guitar, and then other instruments, completing each song in approximately 40 to 45 minutes. "His only purpose, his sole purpose was to prove to himself that he could do it, that he could still make music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Retaining Music Ownership via Roswell Records (1994)
podcast.body: After his Pre-Foo Fighters demos were bootlegged and he was "bestieged with offers," Dave Grohl decided to protect his interests by setting up his own record company, Roswell Records. This was a direct result of his experience with the royalty issues in Nirvana, and his determination to "retain ownership of his music." He informed potential business partners that they would "have to go through" his label. "Dave was determined to retain ownership of his music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Unreleased Christmas 2001 Love Song
podcast.body: In Christmas 2001, Dave Grohl wrote and recorded a unique love song for a girlfriend, which he packaged as a proper CD and gave to her. He reportedly destroyed all other existing copies of the song, and the Foo Fighters have never played it live, with Dave vowing never to release it. The girlfriend, speculated to be Canadian bass player Melissa Oftamar (known for The Smashing Pumpkins and Hole) or American actress Carrie Werher (involved with Dave between 1999 and 2002), is believed to possess the only copy. "It's gotta be a love song that Dave wrote for a one time girlfriend. This was Christmas 2001. He recorded it, had it packaged up like a proper CD and gave it to her and then he reportedly destroyed all the remaining vestiges of that song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Drummer on With Teeth (2005)
podcast.body: Played drums on seven of the 13 songs on Nine Inch Nails' 2005 album "With Teeth." "13 songs, 7 of which featured the drums of some guy named Dave Gold."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Father's Death (2014)
podcast.body: His father, Jim Grohl, passed away from cancer at the age of 75 on August 6, 2014. "Dave saw his father in a regular basis until he died of cancer at the age of 75 on August 6, 2014."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Performance at Concert of Valor (2014)
podcast.body: Dave Grohl performed alongside Bruce Springsteen and Zac Brown at the Concert of Valor in 2014, a special event and fundraiser for American military servicemen and women. "Dave Grohl, Bruce Springsteen, and Zach Brown all playing together in 2014 during a benefit for American military veterans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave of Thrones (2015)
podcast.body: To enable him to continue playing for the remainder of the tour despite his broken leg, Dave Grohl conceived and utilized a customized seat, affectionately called the "Dave of Thrones," which allowed him to play in sync. "ultimately, the cost when he conceived the Dave of Thrones, that customized seat, that allowed him to play in sync for the rest of the tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gothenburg Stage Fall (June 12, 2015)
podcast.body: During a headlining gig at Ullevi Stadium in Gothenburg, Sweden, Dave Grohl fell off the stage during the band's set. He announced to the crowd that he thought he had broken his leg. He initially returned to finish the show after being checked by a doctor. "I think I just broke my leg. I think I really broke my leg."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Leg Break Accident (June 2015)
podcast.body: Dave Grohl broke his leg when he tripped and fell off the stage during a Foo Fighters concert in Guttenberg, Sweden in June 2015, during the second song. He returned to finish the show with his leg bandaged, but the break was severe, leading to canceled shows. "We all know that Dave Grohl broke his leg when he tripped and fell off the stage in Guttenberg, Sweden in June of 2015."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Leg and Ankle Injuries (June 12, 2015)
podcast.body: A post-gig examination after his fall in Gothenburg revealed a badly broken tibia in his right leg and a dislocated ankle. He required surgery, morphine, and later, for his second major injury, five hours of surgery for a left compound distal humerus fracture where the bone was driven through his skin and broken in six pieces, requiring three metal plates and 18 screws. "a post gig exam revealed a badly broken tibia in his right leg along with a dislocated ankle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return to Touring (July 4, 2015)
podcast.body: The Foo Fighters' tour restarted on July 4th in Dave Grohl's hometown of Washington, D.C., coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the release of their first album, allowing the band to continue touring despite his injury using the custom "Dave of Thrones" seat. "The tour, restarted on July 4th in Dave's hometown of Washington, DC."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stage Injury in Sweden (2015)
podcast.body: On June 12, 2015, while performing with the Foo Fighters in Gothenburg, Sweden, Dave Grohl fell approximately 10 feet off the stage onto concrete, announcing, "I think I just broke my leg." The injury, which was severe enough to require surgery and led to the cancellation of several summer tour dates, did not deter Grohl, who returned to the stage later that summer to complete shows from his "Dave of Thrones." "I think I just broke my leg."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 3: (80-71)

podcast.title: Tour Cancellations and Financial Impact (2015)
podcast.body: Following his leg injury in Gothenburg, the Foo Fighters had to cancel several major shows, including two dates at Wembley Stadium and a headliner slot at Glastonbury. The financial loss from these cancellations amounted to approximately $1.25 million per show in lost ticket grosses, plus additional insurance and other costs. "A bunch of shows were canceled, including two massive ones at Wembley Stadium... And a headliner slot at Glastonbury."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Remix of Scream Album (2017)
podcast.body: He remixed Scream's fourth album, *No More Censorship*, which was subsequently reissued in 2017 as part of a Record Store Day event. "That album, by the way, was remixed by Dave, and then reissues part of a record-store day thing in 2017."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: "Dave of Thrones" Performance
podcast.body: Following a severe leg break in June 2015, Dave Grohl continued touring with the Foo Fighters by performing from a unique custom-built "Dave of Thrones." This specialized chair, constructed from guitar necks and adorned with lights, enabled him to play while his leg was immobilized during recovery. "The food fighters did return to the stage later that summer with Dave sitting in his Dave of Thrones, a special over-the-top throne made of guitar necks and equipped with lights."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 3: (80-71)

podcast.title: "Foo Fighters" Name Origin and Dislike
podcast.body: Dave Grohl chose the name "Foo Fighters" for his project after a term used by World War II pilots to describe mysterious "balls of fire over Allied lines" (UFOs). The French word "feu" (fire) influenced the term. He preferred a cloaked, anonymous name, wanting people to think it was a band even though there wasn't one at the time. Despite the name's origins, Dave Grohl "thinks the name Foo Fighters is dumb" and feels "stuck with the name" because the project unexpectedly succeeded. "Dave, by the way, Dave thinks the name Foo Fighters is dumb."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: "What Drives Us" Documentary
podcast.body: Dave Grohl produced a documentary about the experience of touring called "What Drives Us," which featured a soundtrack including a cover of "Nausea" by his daughter Violet and other artists. "Dave's documentary on touring called What Drives Us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 606 East Studio in Virginia Basement
podcast.body: Before the Foo Fighters established their dedicated 606 Studios in Northridge, California, Dave Grohl recorded a couple of the band's albums in his personal basement in Virginia. This informal recording space was affectionately referred to as "606 East." "606 East was Dave's basement in Virginia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Academic Performance in High School
podcast.body: While he achieved straight A's when younger, his academic performance declined significantly by age 17 due to a lack of interest and being a part-time stoner, leading him to transfer schools without improvement. "It wasn't that he wasn't smart. It's just that he didn't care. When he was younger, he got straight A's. Now at age 17, not so much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Admiration for Gary Numan
podcast.body: Dave Grohl, frontman of Foo Fighters, holds Gary Numan in very high regard. "Dave Grohl, the Foo Fighters, thinks he's a god."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Admiration for Springsteen's Stage Performance
podcast.body: Dave Grohl has long admired Bruce Springsteen's stage performance and has consistently strived to emulate that level of energy in his own live shows, often succeeding. "Dave has always admired Springsteen stage performance and for years tried to live up to that kind of energy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Admission of Courtney Love Diss in "I'll Stick Around"
podcast.body: Dave Grohl "copped to this in an interview years later," confirming that the Foo Fighters' 1995 hit "I'll Stick Around" was indeed a diss track aimed at Courtney Love. This admission validated fan interpretations of the song's lyrics. "Grohl copped to this in an interview years later."

Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Age Deception to Play Bars
podcast.body: At age 17, when he joined Scream, he was underage for playing in bars, so he lied about his age, claiming to be 22, to legally perform. "Dave was just 17 at the time, which meant he was under age when he came to playing at bars. So he lied. He said he was 22."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Age at Kurt's Death
podcast.body: Dave Grohl was 25 years old when Kurt Cobain died on April 8, 1994. "Dave was 25."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Age in mid-2010s
podcast.body: Dave Grohl was described as "creeping up on the half-century mark" in the mid-2010s. "Dave Grohl is creeping up on the half-century mark."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Trying to be a Superstar in the 21st Century

podcast.title: Alex Lifeson's Guitar Influence
podcast.body: Dave Grohl admits to regularly incorporating elements of Alex Lifeson's guitar playing into Foo Fighters songs, particularly "anything weird" he does on guitar. He specifically notes that the sustained, ringing notes in riff patterns found in songs like "Times Like These" are directly inspired by listening to Rush. "to this day, I still rip off Alex Lifeson's guitar playing in a lot of Who Fight or Song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alternative Career Aspiration: Helicopter Pilot
podcast.body: If his life had not led him to become a rock star, Dave Grohl's alternative career aspiration was to be a helicopter pilot, indicating an interest beyond music. "If Dave weren't a rock star, he might have followed his other career aspiration of being a helicopter pilot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Amsterdam Squat Tattoo (Age 18)
podcast.body: At 18 years old, Dave Grohl received a tattoo in a squat in Amsterdam from an Italian artist named Andrea, who used a tattoo gun made from a doorbell machine. This tattoo, which contains green and a little bit of red, remains the brightest of all his tattoos to this day. "The one tattoo that's still the most vivid and bright still to this day was a tattoo I got when I was 18 years old in a squat and Amsterdam by this Italian dude named Andrea. And his tattoo gun was made out of a doorbell machine. And it's called if there's green, there's a little bit of red. And that tattoo is still the brightest one of them all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Andrew WK Identical Theory
podcast.body: There is a conspiracy theory that claims Dave Grohl and Andrew WK are the same person. The sole basis for this theory is their similar appearance. "There were those who swear that Dave and party hard guy Andrew WK are the same person."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Australian Driving Ban Incident
podcast.body: Dave Grohl was prohibited from driving in Australia after he was apprehended for driving a motor scooter while intoxicated. "Dave was banned from driving in Australia after being caught drunk on a motor scooter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Big Break with Scream – Joining an Established Band
podcast.body: Dave Grohl's significant career break occurred around 1987 when he was 18 years old. An established local band named Scream announced they were looking for a drummer, and Grohl applied for and secured the position. "Dave's big break came at about 1987 when an established local band called Scream let it be known that they were looking for a drummer So 18-year-old Dave applied and got the job."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bologna Tattoo Experience (Painting for Ink)
podcast.body: While dating a girl from Bologna, Italy, who worked at Art Tattoo Studio, Dave Grohl spent time there. The studio's boss, Marco Pisa, an "incredible tattooist," offered Grohl a tattoo in exchange for painting his studio. Grohl spent a week painting the studio to receive the tattoo on his other side. "So all I wanted was a tattoo from this guy. And he said, okay, I'll give you a tattoo, but you have to paint my studio. So I spent a week like painting his studio and then he gave me another tattoo on this side."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brief Nirvana Quit
podcast.body: Dave Grohl briefly quit Nirvana in 1993 after overhearing Kurt Cobain criticizing his playing style on a flight between gigs. "Dave actually quit Nirvana for a brief time in 1993 because he overheard Kurt back mad mouthing him on a flight between gigs, something about not liking his playing style."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Broken Leg Incident in Sweden
podcast.body: Grohl broke his leg during a performance in Sweden, an incident indirectly linked to Springsteen's influence. On that night, Grohl and his band felt immense pressure to match the intensity of a previous Springsteen show at the same venue, where Springsteen's performance had reportedly cracked the building's foundation. In an attempt to "pull out all the stops," Grohl lost focus and walked off stage, resulting in the injury. "The night that happened, the night Dave broke his leg. He was very aware that Springsteen had played the same venue in Sweden. And that show was so intense that the foundation of the building cracked."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Burying the Late Project
podcast.body: Despite Simple Machines begging him to release *Pocketwatch* on CD, Dave Grohl insisted that the "Late" project be largely buried and forgotten. This was because, as Nirvana began to achieve widespread success, he did not want to be perceived as "crashing the party" with his own material, deeming it "rude." This insistence contributed to the album's lack of attention upon its release. "See, when Nirvana started to take off, he didn't want to be seen as crashing the party with his own stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Childhood Hero Jim Craig & "My Hero" Inspiration
podcast.body: Dave Grohl was a fervent hockey fan, and his first hero was Jim Craig, the starting goalie for the American team that won the gold medal in the 1980 "Miracle on Ice" Olympics against the Soviet Union. Upon learning Craig was from Worcester, Massachusetts, Dave attempted to find and call all Jim Craigs in the area to congratulate them, eventually meeting the Olympic goalie years later at the Winter Olympics. This personal admiration for a relatable, strong individual connects to the inspiration behind his song "My Hero," which celebrates ordinary heroes. "Dave is even today a hockey fan. His very first hero was Jim Craig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Collaboration with Queen of the Stone Age
podcast.body: Dave Grohl (inferred from "de Prolder") is cited as one of the best rock musicians of the last 30 years who has contributed to Queen of the Stone Age's projects. "ha pasado de Prolder."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Queens of The Stone Age  - Villains (información y reseña)

podcast.title: Cousin Tracy Bradford's Punk Introduction
podcast.body: His non-blood relative "cousin," Tracy Bradford, who was two years his senior and lived in Evanston, Illinois, introduced him to authentic punk rock culture. She appeared in bondage pants and motorcycle boots with an anti-P.C. t-shirt, showcasing a record collection including first singles from Misfits and Minor Threat, and connected him to the underground network of fanzines and show flyers from across the country. "She had an antiposti t-shirt and two's punk. I was just like, oh my God, I was so into it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Cousin Tracy's Influence
podcast.body: At age 13, Dave Grohl visited his cousin Tracy in Chicago, who had recently become a punk rocker. She took him to see a punk band at a small, dingy club called The Cubby Bear, across from Wrigley Field. This experience, filled with raw energy and loud music, completely changed his life and redirected his musical aspirations from being a "guitar virtuoso God" on a poster to being a part of a dynamic, accessible punk band. "my cousin Tracy had just turned into a punk rocker and she said, hey, I'm going out tonight. Do you want to see a band?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: DC Hardcore as a Reason to Live
podcast.body: Growing up in Virginia, Dave Grohl found immense personal and musical significance in the DC Hardcore scene, stating it "basically gave him a reason to live." This genre and local scene were so influential that the second episode of the "Sonic Highways" HBO series is dedicated to exploring its impact. "Dave Grohl grew up next door in Virginia. And DC Hardcore basically gave him a reason to live."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Daughter Ruins "Wasting Light" Master Tape
podcast.body: During the recording sessions for the "Wasting Light" album in Dave Grohl's garage, a significant setback occurred when one of his daughters, playing around unsupervised, accidentally ruined a precious analog tape from the session. This incident highlights the raw, hands-on nature of the album's production. "One of the precious tapes from that session was actually ruined by one of Dave's daughters when she was playing around unsupervised."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Departure from Dane Bramage
podcast.body: He abruptly left his band Dane Bramage to join Scream, an offer he "couldn't refuse," which led to hard feelings within Dane Bramage and the band's dissolution. "that band died because Dave bailed. He got an offer that he just couldn't refuse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Desire for More Input in Nirvana
podcast.body: By 1993, Dave Grohl began to agitate for more input, having written his own songs for years and wanting to showcase his abilities within Nirvana. Kurt Cobain, who insisted on receiving 75% of songwriting royalties, blocked these efforts. "Right around this time, this is through 1993, Dave began to agitate for more input. He'd been writing his own songs for years and wanted to showcase some of his abilities with Nirvana."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Devoted Father
podcast.body: Having personally experienced divorce, Dave Grohl is deeply committed to his children, understanding the difficulties it can impose. "Dave came from a family that was torn up by divorce. He's also been divorced himself, so he knows how hard that could be on kids. This is why he's so devoted to his children."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dissatisfaction with Part-time Jobs
podcast.body: He found no happiness in his part-time jobs at Shaky Speeds and Tower Records, as his ultimate desire was to pursue music as a full-time career. "He also wasn't happy working at a couple of part-time jobs at shaky speeds and tower records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Documentary Directing
podcast.body: Dave Grohl has successfully directed documentaries. "Four one-gram view awards. Dave has directed successful documentaries, and the Foo's who played in front of tens of millions of people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dog's Name
podcast.body: His dog was named Bee-Gee, an homage to the Bee Gees. "By the way, Dave's dog's name was Bee-Gee as in the Bee-Gee's."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Dropping Out of High School
podcast.body: With his mother's blessing, he dropped out of high school to tour with Scream. His mother agreed on two conditions: he pay rent and attend night school, though he spent the night school tuition on marijuana instead. "Mum, I'm going to quit high school. I'm not going to graduate. That, as you might guess, did not go over well with the English teacher."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Drum Set at Father's Home
podcast.body: A bedroom at his father's house always contained a drum set, ready for Dave to play whenever he visited, indicating an early exposure and encouragement for his drumming. "there was a bedroom at Jim's house with a drum set waiting for Dave every time he visited."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Multi-track Recording Method
podcast.body: At ages 11 or 12, he devised a method to write and record four-track songs about his dog (Bee-Gee) and school. He used a boombox to record guitar, then played that tape through his mom's stereo while re-recording with the boombox to add drum tracks, layering instruments one by one. "I'd actually write and track songs with my mom's home stereo and my little boombox."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Musical Development
podcast.body: Dave Grohl began making music in his teens, progressing through a series of short-lived bands that were crucial to his development before joining Scream, then Nirvana, and eventually forming Foo Fighters. These early groups included Freak Baby, Fast, and Dane Bramage, as well as Mishmash Impossible, which notably opened for DC's Fugazi. "A Mishmash of short live bands that went nowhere but were very important to Dave's development."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Musical Education – Self-Taught with Records and Pillows
podcast.body: Dave Grohl grew up in Washington D.C., where he learned to play drums and guitar by meticulously studying records from bands like KISS, Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, Black Flag, The Stooges, and Motorhead. While he took guitar lessons first, he taught himself drums by arranging pillows on his bed and practicing with borrowed sticks. "he learned the drums by arranging pillows on his bed and banging them with some borrowed sticks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Musical Influences
podcast.body: His musical journey began with "Frankenstein" by the Edgar Winter Group, which ignited his passion for "big guitar rock." He then explored The Beatles, followed by Rush (given by a cousin), then Devo and Kiss (before B-52s and Devo). Around age 12, he discovered hardcore and punk rock, immersing himself exclusively in these genres for years until around age 16, when he became solely focused on Led Zeppelin. "I just thought, this is the greatest. Then we went out and got some Beatles records. After that, my cousin gave me a Rush record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Song Style
podcast.body: His self-recorded songs from age 11 or 12, created as he was getting into punk rock, likely sounded more like bands such as DOA or Naked Ray Gun rather than The Beatles. "they probably sounded more like, I don't know, DOA or naked ragan or something like that than the Beatles or anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Employment at Tower Records (1980s)
podcast.body: Dave Grohl worked at a Tower Records location in Washington, D.C., during the 1980s. He chose this job because it was one of the few places where he felt his long hair and distinctive fashion sense were accepted, driven by his love for music and the desire to be surrounded by fellow aficionados. "I got a job at Tower Records because that's the only place I could get a job with my f***ing haircut."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the Record Store

podcast.title: Everyman Appeal
podcast.body: Many people point out similarities between Dave Grohl and Bruce Springsteen, particularly their shared "everyman" sort of appeal, often coming across as "regular dudes" despite their fame. "There are many people who have pointed out the similarities between Springsteen and Dave Grohl, especially in that every man sort of appeal both have."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extraordinary Effort for Father-Daughter Dance
podcast.body: While on tour in Australia with the Foo Fighters, Dave Grohl undertook a 15-hour flight from Perth to Los Angeles and another 15-hour return flight (battling severe food poisoning) to attend a father-daughter school dance for his daughter, making it back for a stadium gig with four hours to spare. "Dad flew all the way back from Perth in time to take his daughter to the dance. That's 15 hours. And then he flew right back to Perth, another 15 hours, and made a food stadium gig with four hours to spare."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Father's Career and Influence
podcast.body: His father, Jim Grohl, was a journalist in Warren, Ohio, who gained recognition for covering the Kent State University Anti-Vietnam War student protests on May 4, 1970, where four students were killed by the National Guard. This led to a move to Washington, DC, in 1972 (specifically Springfield, Virginia). Jim later became a speechwriter and campaign manager for Republican politicians, including Senator Robert Taft, Jr., and contributed to the Republican National Convention. "His reporting was so good that it got him on the fast track to a bigger gig in Washington, DC."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Favorite Dr. Seuss Book
podcast.body: Dave Grohl's preferred book by Dr. Seuss is "If I Ran the Rainforest." "Dave's favorite Dr. Sus book is if I ran the rainforest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Favorite Guitar and Influence on Signature Model
podcast.body: Dave Grohl, known for using many guitars, regards the Gibson Trini Lopez ES-335 as his absolute favorite. This specific model served as the inspiration for his own signature guitar. "But his absolute favorite seems to be a Gibson Trinilope's ES335. He has his own signature model now, but that's the guitar that inspired it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: First Album Acquisition
podcast.body: The first album Dave Grohl ever acquired was a K-Tel "hits of the 70s" record, which he obtained after his mother brought home a standard school-issue record player from Fairfax County. "the first album that I got was this K-Tel hits of the 70s record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: First Band Naming (HG Hancock band)
podcast.body: He came up with the name for his first band, the HG Hancock band, a Grade 5 bedroom project with Larry Hinkel. The name was a derivation of their gym teacher's name, Hinkel, combined with an initial for himself, inspired by Lynyrd Skynyrd. "Well H for Hinkel, G for Grohl and Hinkel because, well, that was the name of their gym teacher. It was Dave's idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: First Public Performance (Treebeards)
podcast.body: His first performance for strangers occurred at an open mic night at a local restaurant called Treebeards, alongside his friend Nick Christie. "This is where they got the performance from strangers for the very first time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: First Recorded Appearance at 16
podcast.body: Dave Grohl's debut on record was at the age of 16, playing drums for Mishmash Impossible on their 1985 seven-inch split single. "That's from 1985 with a 16 year old Dave Grohl playing drums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Self-Tattoo Attempt (Age 12-13)
podcast.body: Inspired by a scene in the movie "Christian F." where a character gives herself a stick-and-poke tattoo, Dave Grohl attempted to give himself a Black Flag tattoo on his forearm at the age of 12 or 13. He used a needle and thread from his mother's sewing kit and managed about a third of the thick black design before stopping due to pain, and still retains the "crappy tattoo." "When I saw that, I was like, I can do this myself. So I went to my mother's sewing kit and I got some thread and I got the needle. And I found something and I started giving myself a black flag tattoo. I think I was 12 or 13 years old on my forearm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Touring Experiences (Scream)
podcast.body: Touring America and Europe (including Amsterdam) with Scream at age 17 or 18 marked his first significant travels beyond Chicago. He cherished these experiences, seeing them as freedom and a clear path to his musical passion, despite the lack of money or large audiences. "And then to Europe for the first time. And wow, I'm an Amsterdam, and I'm 18, and I'm free, man. It was cool. It was great."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Foo Fighters Logo Neck Tattoo
podcast.body: Dave Grohl has the Foo Fighters logo tattooed on his neck, which is famously visible on the cover of the band's 1999 album, *There Is Nothing Left to Lose*. "The cover is a black and white photo of the back of Dave's head with the Foo Fighters logo tattooed on his neck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foo Fighters Success
podcast.body: Since the dissolution of Nirvana, Dave Grohl has led the Foo Fighters, releasing nine studio albums that have sold approximately 13 million copies in the US alone and a similar amount worldwide. The band has won four Grammy Awards and played for tens of millions of people. "In the quarter century since the dissolution of Nirvana, there have been nine Foo Fighters studio albums, something about 13 million copies in the US alone, and about the same amount worldwide."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grammy Award as a Door Stop
podcast.body: Despite winning a Grammy Award for the Foo Fighters' album "There Is Nothing Left to Lose," Dave Grohl initially used the prestigious trophy as a door stop for his bedroom. It was later moved from this unconventional spot to a shelf, its more traditional place. "Dave used his Grammy as a door stop for his bedroom for a while but it's since graduated to a shelf."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Guinness World Record for Heaviest Drumsticks
podcast.body: Dave Grohl is linked to a Guinness World Record through a tribute in his birthplace of Warren, Ohio. The town honored him by erecting a giant pair of drumsticks in its town center, which weigh 902 pounds, officially making them the heaviest drumsticks in the world. "His birthplace of Warren O'Hyle honored him by erecting a giant pair of drumsticks in the town center. They weigh 902 pounds, making them the heaviest in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Impact on Nirvana's Sound
podcast.body: Dave Grohl joined Nirvana as drummer between their first and second albums, injecting a "serious kick" into their sound and completing their lineup. His arrival was likened to Ringo Starr belatedly joining The Beatles. "Grohl gave Nirvana a serious kick."

Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Initial Reluctance on "Best of You" Inclusion
podcast.body: Dave Grohl initially did not want the song "Best of You" to be included on the "In Your Honor" album. Despite his reservations, he was ultimately persuaded that incorporating the track into the record was the correct decision. "Dave didn't really want that song on the record, but he was ultimately convinced that it might be the right thing to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Intensified Led Zeppelin Fascination
podcast.body: Although he'd heard Led Zeppelin on AM radio, his true fascination with the band intensified after Chip Donaldson moved in. This was further solidified when neighborhood stoners gave him the first two Zeppelin albums, leading him to consider them "his band" and becoming a huge fan of John Bonham. "And it was through Chip that Dave was first properly exposed to Led Zeppelin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: John Bonham Inspired Tattoo
podcast.body: Grohl, being a drummer, was obsessed with John Bonham and had the Led Zeppelin drummer's iconic three circles tattooed on his upper arm, later adding a tribal design over it. "I was obsessed with John Bonham, Mike, right? As a drummer. So I got the three circles and then I put some tribal thing over it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: John Bottom Influence and Powerful Playing
podcast.body: Dave Grohl is known for his exceptionally hard-hitting drumming style, which is directly attributed to his drumming idol, John Bottom of Led Zeppelin. Bottom was also a renowned heavy hitter, and Grohl effectively channeled this influence into his own powerful playing. "That's because his drumming idol is Led Zeppelin's John Bottom, another really heavy hitter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Kurt's Consideration to Ban from Unplugged
podcast.body: Prior to the MTV Unplugged taping, Kurt Cobain considered banning Dave Grohl from the performance because he doubted Dave's ability to play for the acoustic setting. "And until the band actually took the stage for the taping of the MTV and Plug broadcast, Kurt had been thinking of banning Dave from the gig because he didn't think he was up to it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late Project & Jenny Toomey Crush
podcast.body: Dave Grohl recorded his solo album *Pocketwatch* under the alias "Late" for Simple Machines, a "cheapo label" run out of a house in Arlington, Virginia. One of the people running the label was Jenny Toomey, and Dave had a "huge crush on here," which "might be the only reason he agreed to let her label put out that cassette." "Dave had a huge crush on here, which might be the only reason he agreed to let her label put out that cassette."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Led Zeppelin Tattoos
podcast.body: He has three Led Zeppelin tattoos. The first, John Bonham's three-circle runic symbol from the fourth Led Zeppelin album, he tattooed himself at age 16. The second was done by an amateur artist in Amsterdam, and the third was paid for with his first check from Nirvana ($400), which he also used to buy a Nintendo and a BB gun. "Not only did he become a huge fan of drummer John Bonham, but today he has three Led Zeppelin tattoos, the first of which he did himself when he was 16."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Mother's Handmade Memorabilia for 606 Studios
podcast.body: In a personal touch at Foo Fighters' 606 Studios, Dave Grohl's mother created throw pillows for the studio's couches using his old concert t-shirts. This memorabilia, alongside other Nirvana and Foo Fighters items, filled the building, much of which Dave previously stored in his mother's basement. "The most charming thing I saw were the throw pillows on the couches. They were made by Dave's mum from his old concert t-shirts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Mother's Profession and Support
podcast.body: His mother, Virginia Grohl, worked as an English and drama teacher at Thomas Jefferson High School. She notably supported his decision to drop out of high school to pursue music, albeit with conditions. "Mum, Virginia Grohl, got a job as an English and drama teacher at Thomas Jefferson High School."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Musical Collaborations with Daughter Violet
podcast.body: Dave Grohl has often brought his oldest daughter, Violet, on stage to sing with him, and they have recorded together. "Dave is brought as oldest of three daughters' violets on stage with him to sing on a number of occasions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Neil Peart as an Idol
podcast.body: Dave Grohl identifies Rush drummer Neil Peart as a significant influence, stating that Peart was "my guy on the wall" when discussing his early musical heroes. This highlights the impact of Peart's drumming on Grohl's own musical development and appreciation. "Meal Perk was my guy on the wall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nirvana Role
podcast.body: During his time with Nirvana (fall 1990 to April 1994), Dave Grohl was primarily the drummer, keeping time for Kurt Cobain's songs and singing some backup vocals. "Back in 1994, Dave was just the drummer. He kept time for Kurt songs and sang some backup vocals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Normal Residence in Encino, California
podcast.body: Dave Grohl resides in a quiet, seemingly ordinary neighborhood in Encino, California. His home features a white picket fence and a simple sign reading "The Grohls" out front, notably lacking security measures like gates, guards, or fences, reflecting a preference for a normal lifestyle. "These days, Dave lives in a very quiet area of Encino, California. The south looks really normal, complete with a white picket fence and a sign that simply says the growls out front. No gates, no guards, no fences."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Nirvana Leadership – Foo Fighters
podcast.body: Following the death of Kurt Cobain, Dave Grohl surprised many by stepping out from behind the drum kit. He transitioned to the role of leader, singer, and guitarist for his new band, the Foo Fighters, demonstrating his skills as a musician, songwriter, and singer that many had not expected. "After Kurt's death Dave stepped up from behind the kid as the leader singer and guitarist of the foo fighters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Preference for Cheese
podcast.body: Dave Grohl has a pronounced fondness for cheese, stating that he "likes cheese. A lot." It is suggested that offering him cheese is a reliable way to get on his good side. "And if you want to get on Dave's good side, get him some cheese. He likes cheese. A lot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Preferred Guitar for Foo Fighters Recordings
podcast.body: Dave Grohl's absolute favorite guitar is a 1967 ES-335. This particular instrument has been exclusively used to record every single guitar part on every Foo Fighters song ever produced. "His absolute favorite guitar is a 1967 ES-335. It's been used to track every single guitar part on every single Fufiter song ever recorded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prior Relationship with Jennifer Finch
podcast.body: Dave Grohl was a former boyfriend of Jennifer Finch, a member of the band L7, who was also a friend of Courtney Love. This connection within the music scene facilitated communication and exchanges between Courtney Love and Kurt Cobain. "Courtney was friends with Jennifer Finch of the band L7, who was a former girlfriend of Dave Grohl."

podcast.body: The probability of Dave Grohl's specific existence has been estimated to be at the very lowest one in two quadrillion six hundred eighty-five trillion. This number, derived from an unscientific extrapolation of Dr. Ali Bin-Azer's estimate of the uniqueness of existence, highlights the extreme improbability of any individual's unique being. "the chances of Dave Grohl being Dave Grohl is at the very lowest one in two quadrillion six hundred eighty five trillion."

srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Progressive Political Stance
podcast.body: Growing up under the influence of his hardcore conservative, Reaganite father, Dave Grohl ultimately adopted a more progressive political approach, partly because his parents' divorce in his early childhood prevented his father's lifelong conservatism from fully impacting him. "Therefore, it's safe to say that Dad's lifelong political conservatism didn't really have a chance to rub off on Dave, who eventually adopted a more progressive approach."

podcast.title: Pseudo-Stepdad's Record Collection
podcast.body: His mother's boyfriend, Chip Donaldson, who was an English teacher and Vietnam veteran, moved in with his own record collection featuring music from the late 1960s and early 1970s, including artists like The Rolling Stones, Bob Dylan, and Grateful Dead. "It featured a lot of stuff from the late 60s and early 70s. Stones, Dylan, grateful dad, that kind of thing."

srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Quit School at 17
podcast.body: Dave Grohl made the decision to quit school at the age of 17 to join the Washington D.C.-based band Scream. This early career move marked his full commitment to music. "Dave quit school at age 17 to join a DC band called Scream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recruitment of Sunny Day Real Estate Rhythm Section
podcast.body: Dave Grohl recruited the entire rhythm section from the band Sunny Day Real Estate, who then became a significant part of the Foo Fighters' lineup. "decided that they'd rather work for Dave Grohl and became one half of the food fighters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Refusal of Wider Release for "Pocket Watch"
podcast.body: Despite bootlegs appearing from places like Italy, Dave Grohl refused Jenny Toomey's requests to officially release "Pocket Watch" on vinyl or CD. He stated a preference to keep it exclusively as a cassette-only album, limiting its official distribution. "When bootlegs started appearing from places like Italy, she begged Dave to allow her to release the album on vinyl, or on CD, but Dave said, no, no, no, I would just rather keep it as a cassette thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reputation as "Nicest Man in Rock"
podcast.body: Dave Grohl has garnered a widespread reputation and is described as truly deserving the title of "the nicest man in rock," based on observed interactions and his overall demeanor. "Dave really does deserve the title as the nicest man in rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 3

podcast.title: Rush's 2112 Introduction
podcast.body: Dave Grohl's cousin gave him the Rush album "2112" when he was in third grade, which was his first exposure to music beyond The Beatles and AM Radio. He was captivated by the unique sound and the prominent drums, but felt apprehensive about sharing it with friends due to the band's appearance, including their kimonos and Alex Lifeson's "camel toe." "I remember my, I had a cousin, another cousin, give me 2112, Um, maybe when I was about, I remember I was in third grade and um, up until that point, it had pretty much only been in the Beatles and AM Radio for me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Self-Doubt in Nirvana
podcast.body: During his time in Nirvana, Dave Grohl had significant self-doubt about his musical abilities, particularly his singing voice and songwriting skills. He believed his own material was "substandard," leading him to record most of his personal music in secret and only share it with a select few. This self-perception, combined with the understanding that Nirvana was primarily "Kurt's band," limited his contributions to the band's songwriting, despite his innate musical talent. "He didn't like a singing voice, and he didn't think he was any good as a songwriter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 2

podcast.title: Self-Perceived Luck
podcast.body: Despite his talent and ambition, Dave Grohl believes he is one of the luckiest humans alive, acknowledging that many factors beyond his control had to align perfectly for his career to unfold as it has. "He knows he's among the luckiest humans alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Signature Gibson DG-355
podcast.body: Dave Grohl's affection for his ES-355 guitar led him to collaborate with Gibson in 2005 to design his own signature model, the DG-355. This guitar is notably based on a model that Trini Lopez utilized during the 1960s. "Dave Grohl loves his ES-355 so much that he got together with Gibson in 2005 to design a signature guitar, and it's called, of course, the DG-355."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Singing Lead in Scream
podcast.body: He sang lead vocals on the song "God's Look Down" for Scream's fifth album, *Fumble*, despite feeling "totally vulnerable," "naked," and "exposed" when singing lead, preferring the anonymity of a drummer. "I just always felt really weird about singing, like I didn't mind singing backups, but when it's my voice out front, that's when it gets creepy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

podcast.title: Speculated Post-Nirvana Life (if Kurt Lived)
podcast.body: It is speculated that Dave Grohl, freed from being Kurt's timekeeper, would have continued with Foo Fighters, with little change to his trajectory. "Dave Grohl finally freed from being just Kurt's timekeeper would have gone about his merry way with the food fighters. I can't see that being much different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Survival of Late Songs
podcast.body: Over the years, though, songs from Dave Grohl's Late project have surfaced in various forms. In addition to bootlegs, tracks have appeared on 7-inch compilations, and some were re-recorded and renamed for Foo Fighters releases, demonstrating the enduring influence of his early solo work. "Over the years, though, songs from late have shown up. In addition to the bootlegs, tracks have appeared on 7-inch compilations, somewhere we recorded, and renamed for Foo Fighters releases."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Taking Over Drumming Duties – Freak Baby
podcast.body: Dave Grohl's full-time transition to drums came when he was a member of the band Freak Baby. The original drummer was performing so poorly that Grohl decided to take over the drumming responsibilities himself. "Because when he was in a band called Freak Baby the drummer was so bad that Dave just kind of took over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Temporary Departure and QOTSA Drumming
podcast.body: After Taylor Hawkins's near-fatal overdose in 2001, Dave Grohl stepped away from the Foo Fighters to "sort his head out." During this period, he briefly became the drummer for Queens of the Stone Age. "That's when he briefly became drummer for Queens of the Stone Age."

podcast.title: Transition from Guitarist to Drummer
podcast.body: Dave Grohl did not start his musical journey as a drummer; his first instrument was the guitar, which he began playing at age 12. During high school, he played in various bands, and it was in one particular group, Freak Baby, that he transitioned from playing guitar to drums. He remained primarily a drummer until the dissolution of Nirvana. "His first instrument was the guitar, something he first picked up at age 12."

podcast.title: UFO and Science Fiction Fascination
podcast.body: Dave Grohl has had a lifelong fascination with UFOs and science fiction, dating back to his childhood. He would lie in his front yard waiting for UFOs, had "crazy UFO dreams," and loved science fiction toys and action figures. This interest influenced his choice of the name "Foo Fighters" for his band and "Roswell Records" for his label, both referencing UFO phenomena. "Well, for a long time, since I was a kid, I'd always been really fascinated with UFOs."

xref.body: Despite his rock star status, Dave Grohl's all-time favorite vehicle is a 1965 Ford Falcon van. He discovered the van in the Arizona desert with three flat tires, purchased it, and had it customized by King T's Customs in California. xref.title: Dave Grohl's Father Covered the Kent State Massacre (May 1970)
xref.body: In 1970, the Grohl family lived in Niles, Ohio (near Columbus). Dave's father James Grohl was a reporter for the Scripps News Agency and was assigned to cover anti-Vietnam War protests at Kent State University on May 1, 1970 — and was present when the National Guard opened fire, killing four students. James Grohl won several awards for his on-the-spot reporting, earning a major promotion and reassignment to Washington D.C., where Dave grew up and discovered music. "Had it not been for the National Guard killing four unarmed students at Kent State, who knows if we'd ever have heard of Dave Grohl?"

xref.title: Dave Grohl Joined Nirvana Because His Band's Bassist Broke Up with His Girlfriend (1990)
xref.body: Dave dropped out of high school to tour with DC punk band Scream for about three years. In the summer of 1990, bassist Skeater Thompson flaked out mid-tour in Los Angeles over the loss of his girlfriend, canceling multiple shows. Dave was left penniless (temporarily crashing with three female mud wrestlers) and doing cash tiling work for food money. He called Melvins leader King Buzzo (Kurt Cobain's idol), whom he'd met in Europe, who told him Kurt had a band needing a drummer. Dave flew to Seattle on September 21, 1990; four days later he auditioned and passed. Dave later wrote a song about Skeater Thompson called "Just Another Story About Skeater Thompson," available only on a cassette-only release made under the name "Late" in late 1990, titled *Pocket Watch*. "Dave has never forgotten Skeater Thompson and how thankful he is that Skeater had such bad girlfriend trouble."

xref.title: Death by Suicide (April 5, 1994)
xref.body: Kurt Cobain died in the early morning of Tuesday, April 5, 1994, by suicide via shotgun, preceded by a massive heroin overdose. His body was found approximately two weeks later, on April 8. His family and friends were aware he was in trouble, especially after a previous suicide attempt at a hotel in Rome. On March 25, 1994, an intervention was held at his Seattle home with his wife Courtney Love, bandmates Chris Novoselic and Dave Grohl, touring guitarist Pat Smear, and members of Nirvana's management and legal team, lasting five hours. He seemed convinced to seek help and flew to LA on March 30 to check into the Exodus Recovery Center. However, he left on April 1 (Good Friday) by scaling a six-foot wall, flew back to Seattle, and disappeared. His final note, addressed to his imaginary friend "Boddah," was found in his pocket after he injected a large amount of Mexican black tar heroin and then used a Remington shotgun to kill himself in the greenhouse at his home. "He had injected so much heroin that he probably never even heard the gun go off."

xref.body: Following their performance at Terminal 1 in Munich on March 1, 1994, the remainder of Nirvana's European tour was cancelled. This decision was made because Kurt Cobain was deemed unfit to continue, suffering from bronchitis and a sore throat. The other band members, Krist Novoselic and Dave Grohl, also needed a vacation, with Novoselic returning to Seattle and Grohl remaining in Germany to work on a film soundtrack. The group included Courtney, Nirvana bandmates Chris Novoselic and Dave Grohl, touring Nirvana guitarist Pat Smear, and members of Nirvana's management and legal team. This intervention lasted for five hours and was an attempt to confront Kurt about his problems and convince him to seek help. "This intervention lasted for five hours. When it was all over, Kurt seemed convinced, and he flew to LA on the 30th to check into a rehab unit known for straightening out strong-out celebrities."

On March 30, he checked into the Exodus Recovery Center in Los Angeles but departed just two days later on April 1, scaling a guard wall despite having checked in voluntarily. "That meeting lasted five hours. Kurt was convinced to try rehab and arrangements were made."

xref.title: Taylor Hawkins' Death (March 25, 2022)
xref.body: Foo Fighters drummer Taylor Hawkins died suddenly on March 25, 2022, in Bogota, Colombia, just before the band was set to headline a festival. At approximately 7:40 PM on that Friday night, a call was made from a Four Seasons property reporting a guest with severe chest pains, but EMS responders arrived too late. Officially, he died from complications related to an enlarged heart (cardiomegaly), which weighed 600 grams (compared to a normal 300 grams). Although his doctors were aware of his enlarged heart for years, attributing it to his active lifestyle of surfing, biking, and intense drumming, little other information regarding his death was released, due to an "airtight" news blackout imposed by the band and management. This lack of information fueled conspiracy theories, though sources suggested a congenital problem exacerbated by exhaustion, as Hawkins had reportedly been feeling "rough" in the months leading up to the South American tour. His death profoundly impacted Dave Grohl, the Foo Fighters, and millions of fans globally. "Taylor was dead. Officially, he died of complications involving an enlarged heart, something called cardiomagalley."

xref.title: 606 Studios: The All-Purpose Hub (Northridge, California)
xref.body: In 2005, following the success of the "One by One" album, the Foo Fighters invested $750,000 to establish their 8,000-square-foot 606 Studios (also known as 606 West) in Northridge, California. Dave Grohl describes it as the "all-purpose Foo Fighters hub" where they rehearse, store gear, record albums, and host press events. The studio, originally a warehouse and once the home of a woman being stalked, was inspired by ABBA's Polar Studios and prominently features the recording console from the legendary Sound City Studios, used by Nirvana, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Rage Against the Machine, Slipknot, and Tom Petty. "By the time the Fuzc got to the one by one album in 2005, they had enough money to invest in their own recording studio in Northridge, California. They call it 606 Studios."

xref.title: Initial Anonymity
xref.body: When Dave Grohl first started the "Foo Fighters" project, he intentionally chose the name to cloak everything "as if it were an unknown band from Seattle." At the time of the initial demos, there was "actually no band," only Dave playing all the instruments, and he wanted people to perceive it as a group. "Dave could have called the project after himself, but he preferred cloaking everything as if it were an unknown band from Seattle, even though there was actually no band at the time."

xref.title: John Bonham's Drumming Influence
xref.body: John Bonham, the drummer for Led Zeppelin, was known for his hard-hitting style, which Dave Grohl himself followed in. This style was a benchmark for powerful rock drumming. "Dave, no, of course, was a hard hitter in the tradition of Led Zeppelin's John Bonham."

xref.title: John Bonham's Runic Symbol

xref.title: Killing Joke's Reaction and Dave Grohl's Friendship
xref.body: While similarities between "Come As You Are" and Killing Joke's "Eighties" were noted by Killing Joke's singer Jazz Coleman, it's unclear if legal action was taken. Some believe it was initiated and then stopped after Kurt Cobain's death in 1994, while others say Killing Joke's respect for Nirvana prevented it. Ultimately, "all is forgiven" as Dave Grohl is "great friends with killing joke" and has "performed and toured with him." "Whatever the case, all is forgiven in the Nirvana killing joke situation."

xref.title: Kurt's Band Dynamic
xref.body: Nirvana was widely known as "Kurt's band," with Kurt Cobain serving as the leader, singer, and primary songwriter. This dynamic was acknowledged by Dave Grohl, who understood he had "stumbled into a lottery win" and was hesitant to disrupt the established structure. This power dynamic contributed to Dave's self-doubt and limited his opportunities to contribute his own songs to the band's official releases. "First of all, Nirvana was Kurt's band. He was the leader, singer, songwriter, Dave knew that he stumbled into a lottery win and wasn't about to mess with the situation."

xref.title: Kurt's Reluctance to Include Dave Grohl in Unplugged

"And until the band actually took the stage for the taping of the MTV and Plug broadcast, Kurt had been thinking of banning Dave from the gig because he didn't think he was up to it."

xref.title: Leaving Alanis Morissette for Foo Fighters
xref.body: While touring with Alanis Morissette, Taylor Hawkins frequently crossed paths with the Foo Fighters at summer festivals and quickly bonded with Dave Grohl. Alanis eventually asked him when he was going to quit and join the Foo Fighters, which he did, despite Alanis being a bigger act at the time. "It got to the point where Alannis asked, when are you just going to quit and join the food fighters?"

xref.title: Name Origin (WWII Pilots)
xref.body: The name "Foo Fighters" was chosen by Dave Grohl, derived from a term used by World War II pilots. These pilots described "mysterious balls of fire over Allied lines" as "Foo Fighters," a slang term for UFOs. The French word for fire, "feu" (F-E-U), was noted as a potential influence. "He called his project Foo Fighters after a term used by World War II pilots to describe mysterious balls of fire over Allied lines."

xref.title: Near Dissolution After Taylor Hawkins's Overdose
xref.body: The Foo Fighters nearly disbanded after drummer Taylor Hawkins's severe heroin overdose in London in 2001, which put him in a two-week coma. Frontman Dave Grohl was unwilling to endure another situation where a band member might die, leading to uncertainty about the band's future and a temporary hiatus for Grohl. "But it was anything but in fact that was almost the end of the Foo Fighters. Dave Groha had no intention of going through another situation where a band may die."

xref.title: Post-Nirvana Feud with Courtney Love
xref.body: A significant feud developed between Dave Grohl and Courtney Love after Kurt Cobain's death. The first public evidence of bad blood was a 1999 interview where Dave Grohl, when asked for his favorite Hole song, replied "Teenage Horror" because it was "the one I know Courtney actually wrote," implying she didn't write others. Courtney Love subsequently attacked Dave in the media over legal disputes concerning Nirvana's music, accusing him of being sexually obsessed with Kurt Cobain and claiming he hired Taylor Hawkins as Foo Fighters' drummer because of Hawkins' resemblance to Kurt. "The first evidence I can find of some kind of bad blood was an interview Dave gave in 1999, a few years after the food fighters got going."

xref.title: Post-Nirvana Success – Dave Grohl's New Role
xref.body: After the death of Kurt Cobain and the end of Nirvana, Dave Grohl formed the Foo Fighters, taking on the roles of leader, lead singer, and guitarist. The band achieved considerable success, surprising many who hadn't realized the extent of Grohl's musical, songwriting, and singing talents during his time as Nirvana's drummer. "After Kurt's death Dave stepped up from behind the kid as the leader singer and guitarist of the foo fighters and Well, they've done okay, huh."

xref.title: Postcard to Dave Grohl
xref.body: Seven Year Bitch sent a postcard to Dave Grohl following Kurt Cobain's suicide, understanding the grief he was experiencing. The message on the postcard encouraged him to continue with music: "We know what you're going through. The desire to play music is gone for now, but it will return. Don't worry." This message was a "deciding factor" in convincing Dave to keep making music. "It read, We know what you're going through. The desire to play music is gone for now, but it will return. Don't worry."

xref.title: Punk Rock Accessibility Model
xref.body: Dave Grohl identifies The Ramones as a prime example of punk rock's simplicity and accessibility, noting that their three-chord structure made music seem attainable for aspiring musicians who felt intimidated by virtuoso rock gods. This ease of entry allowed young people to start bands and write about relevant local issues. "And then you hear a Ramones song and it's three chords and you can do that and then you have friends that might not play drums like Buddy Rich or but they can play drums like the guy from the Sex Bistels or because it's so simple, it becomes available to you like, oh cool, well, I could start a band if we do it like this."

xref.body: Taylor Hawkins was considered by many, next to Dave Grohl, to be the most important member of the Foo Fighters, a beloved fan favorite.
